Katalog Berita (Halaman 7/57)

#10144. Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes

A developer building on Google Cloud today can scaffold a long-horizon memory agent from the terminal, install a retail vertical skill into a coding assistant with one line, and deploy a fully-wired production service to Cloud Run, Agent Runtime, Agent Garden, or Gemini Enterprise app — all from the same curated source tree. That tree is google/adk-recipes, the restructured successor to google/adk-samples that now serves Agent Platform from a single source of truth.

ADK recipes are agent-friendly: we've made it easy for your agents to 1) discover relevant recipes for various agent use cases, and 2) install and use them automatically from your favorite harness.

google/adk-recipes splits its content into three top-level folders: core/ for reference patterns curated by the Agents CLI and DevRel teams, plugins/ for installable vertical skills packaged as Plugin Recipes conforming to the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 spec, and contrib/ for end-to-end deployable services across five languages. Every piece has been designed with machine readability as the primary consideration.

What follows is a walkthrough of the repository's shape, three worked examples (one per layer), and a reflection on what the new structure enables.

Three top-level roots, each anchored on one reader action:

Every recipe ships a validated manifest.yaml, an AGENTS.md that tells the coding assistant opening it what the recipe is and how to use it, and (for contrib/ and plugins/) a Dockerfile plus a runnability test. CI enforces the standards on every PR, and a suite of coding-assistant skills in the repo (prepare-python-recipe, generate-manifest, github-pr-review, and others) does most of the preparation, so your agent can scaffold, validate, and submit a recipe end-to-end.

Every AGENTS.md, every manifest.yaml, every SKILL.md is written primarily for the AI coding assistant that will open the repo on your behalf; README.md files are what humans still read. The handbook glossary captures the dual framing: "Recipe — a runnable agent example (or importable agent module) under core/, contrib/, or plugins/, consumed by ADK developers and coding agents alike."

adk-recipes serves as the single source of truth for ADK content across the three Agent Platform surfaces that consume it. Each reads the repository through its own protocol.

Agents CLI reads core/. When a developer runs uvx --from google-agents-cli agents-cli create my-agent, Agents CLI can scaffold on demand a core/ recipe. The CLI, launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next, exposes the full scaffold → deploy → evaluate → publish lifecycle; the base content it serves comes from our recipes. Horizon, the reference harness we examine below, is an example pattern Agents CLI treats as a production template.

Agent Garden features a curated selection. The developer-facing path into the repository is a pull request to contrib/: a recipe lands in GitHub, becomes part of the public ADK ecosystem, and from that moment is discoverable by other developers and by coding assistants reading the repository. Appearing in the Agent Garden gallery is a separate editorial decision made by the Agent Garden team, which curates a subset of recipes and promotes them to the public catalog on their own cadence. Once an agent is in the gallery, any developer in a Google Cloud project gets a one-click install.

Beyond these primary surfaces, Google Cloud's own infrastructure components appear as building blocks inside the recipes themselves. Horizon uses Agent Platform Sandboxes for per-user sandboxing, Memory Bank for durable memory, and Agent Platform Sessions for session state. The retail product-search Plugin Recipe uses Vector Search 2.0 on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform paired with BigQuery. The retail virtual-tryon Plugin Recipe uses Gemini image models for still composites and Veo 3.1 Reference-to-Video for animated outputs. The recipes do not just live alongside Agent Platform; they document it in use.

For developers working with coding assistants outside Google Cloud's tooling (Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and others), Plugin Recipes additionally install through the open npx skills CLI maintained by vercel-labs.

Building an agent that can handle a single conversation is a well-understood problem. Building one that holds its own across days of interaction, remembering what the user did yesterday and planning tasks for tomorrow, is a materially different undertaking. The hard parts of such a long-horizon system are the same regardless of what the agent is being built to do: cross-session memory, per-user sandboxing of tool execution, secrets management, guardrails against runaway behaviour, and the orchestration primitives that make multi-step tasks resumable. Horizon, which lives at core/python/long-horizon-harness, is the reference harness we built to collect these primitives in one place.

The shortest path from a fresh clone to a running Horizon instance:

make deploy rolls the backend to Cloud Run through Terraform; make destroy tears it back down. Horizon's evaluation suite lives in tests/eval/evalsets/ as eighteen named behavioural rubrics covering memory recall, injection-based exfiltration attempts, guardrail halting under adversarial input, tool-selection discipline, and a journey-level plot-artifact evaluation. The rubrics are executed with uv run pytest tests/eval.

A first chat turn against the running backend confirms the memory layer is wired correctly:

Horizon is the harness we give coding assistants to study before building something harder. When a developer asks their assistant to build an agent that must run across days of interaction, the right next step is uvx google-agents-cli create with Horizon as the scaffold, and the rest of the harness falls into place.

Horizon encodes a reference pattern. It does not encode a vertical. For that, the second layer of the repository holds Plugin Recipes, each addressing a specific industry domain. The first vertical fully covered in this launch is retail, available under plugins/retail/.

The Plugin Recipe format sits on top of the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 specification published at agent-plugins.org, an open standard for packaging installable AI skills across coding assistants. The specification defines a plugin as a bundle of one or more skills with a top-level plugin.json manifest declaring name, version, license, and ownership. Each skill is a self-contained folder with a SKILL.md conversational installer, a README.md, an EVAL.yaml of quality gates, and the scripts and assets the skill needs to do its work. The retail plugin's layout is:

Two skills ship in this plugin today. The first, retail-product-search, builds an ADK agent with a vector-search retrieval tool backed by Vector Search 2.0 on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and a BigQuery catalog. The skill handles the entire pipeline: ingesting a CSV or JSON catalog into BigQuery, generating multimodal and text embeddings with Vertex AI Embeddings, building the Vector Search collection, scaffolding the ADK agent with a retrieve_docs tool, and deploying to Cloud Run. The agent is deliberately single-agent: one root_agent with one retrieval tool and no coordinator layer. The semantic complexity sits in the retrieval pipeline and the evaluator rubric, not in agent-to-agent communication; adding orchestration layers would obscure the pattern rather than clarify it.

The second skill, retail-virtual-tryon, generates a photorealistic composite of a model wearing or holding a product, with an optional eight-second studio catwalk video on top. It uses gemini-2.5-flash-image by default, falling back to gemini-2.5-pro-image when editorial quality matters more than latency. For video it uses veo-3.1-generate-001 in Reference-to-Video mode, conditioning the generated motion on the still produced by the image pipeline. The skill ships a pre-flight product-cutout classifier and configurable safety levels, operational details that become obvious after the third real production deployment.

Both skills install into any coding assistant that reads skills with a single command:

The --full-depth flag instructs the CLI to walk past its default top-level lookup and discover the nested plugins/retail/skills/ structure. The install lands in ~/.agents/skills// and is symlinked into every detected coding assistant on the local machine:

The skill ecosystem is designed to compose. The retail-product-search SKILL.md instructs the host coding assistant to pull two companion skills from google/skills if they are not already installed, keeping cross-cutting concerns like BigQuery basics and Gemini API usage in one place and reusable by multiple vertical plugins.

Once installed, the coding assistant reads SKILL.md and initiates a Q-MODE interview. For retail-product-search, Quick Start is two questions (GCP project ID and the path to product data, with sensible defaults for both); Full Setup adds two more covering product-fields level and GCP region. By the end of the interview the skill has written a ./design-spec.md reflecting the project's actual shape and executed scripts/setup.py to land the catalog in BigQuery, generate the embeddings, build the Vector Search collection, and run EVAL.yaml against the result. If the rubric and assertion checks fall below the 80 percent passing target, the skill halts and surfaces the specific failures.

An end-to-end setup run on the bundled five-product demo catalog produces:

A live retrieval against the collection the skill has just provisioned returns:

The virtual-tryon skill is faster to demonstrate interactively. A direct call to generate_tryon_image with a user portrait and a product image produces the photorealistic composite shown at the top of this section in roughly ten seconds. The same inputs piped through generate_tryon_video and Veo Reference-to-Video turn that still into an eight-second studio catwalk animation of the composite in motion.

The pipeline is category-agnostic. Swapping the product image for a pair of sunglasses, with product_category='eyewear', invokes the same generate_tryon_image call and produces a composite in the correct category without any further configuration:

Retail is the first vertical fully covered in this format. Additional verticals will land as their own folders under plugins/, following the same anatomy and the same Agent Plugins specification, so developers can expect a consistent install experience across industries.

The contrib/ layer is where ADK recipes become end-to-end deployable services. Twelve Python agents live there today, spanning the kinds of applications ADK is typically used to build in practice: finance (financial advisor, small-business loan processor), evaluation (LLM auditor), document and knowledge pipelines (high-volume document analyzer, multiformat hybrid RAG), content and brand (brand-aligned presentations, brand-search optimization, on-brand genmedia), retail (product search, virtual try-on), and framework examples (agent-skills tutorial, staged UI widgets). Java, Go, TypeScript, and Kotlin each carry smaller sets. Every entry in contrib/ is a worked example of how a core/ pattern or a plugins/ skill becomes a running service.

To make the relationship between a plugin and its deployable counterpart concrete, take contrib/python/retail-product-search as the example. The retail plugin from the previous section walked a developer through a conversational install that provisioned the Vector Search collection, the BigQuery catalog, and the embeddings. The contrib agent is the deployable counterpart: a long-running service that reads from that collection and answers natural-language shopping queries over it. The plugin owns the one-shot setup; the contrib agent owns the service shape. Both are maintained by the same team to stay synchronised, and the agent's README directs new users to run the plugin's setup first:

Once the collection (retail-skill-products-collection) is populated, the agent is cloned out of contrib/python/retail-product-search, pointed at a GCP project, and surfaced on one of five deployment personas controlled by boolean flags in .env.

Once the deployment is live, the agent exposes a hosted shopping-assistant endpoint. The same retrieve_docs tool we called directly from Python now sits behind a chat interface, reachable through the deployed Reasoning Engine or, during development, through the ADK Web UI. The exact same agent code answering the exact same shopping query, run locally for inspection:

The agent graph on the left of the UI confirms the single-agent architecture (product_search_agent → retrieve_docs). The right panel traces each tool invocation. The response grounds in a real catalog row from Vector Search: "Sony Wireless Headphones · Price: $199.99 · Brand: Sony · Rating: 4.5/5 (50 in stock) · Premium noise-cancelling over-ear headphones featuring an impressive 30-hour battery life." No products are hallucinated; the Vector Search collection on top of BigQuery is the source of truth.

That is what the retail plugin gives a team. The plugin encodes the data-pipeline setup once, through a conversational install any coding assistant can execute. The contrib agent is the running service, deployable in five shapes, that any organisation can take as a starting point and swap in its own catalog. The virtual-tryon counterpart in contrib/python/retail-virtual-tryon follows the same pattern: a smaller root agent that orchestrates try_on_product_image and try_on_product_video tools, deployable in the same five shapes, built on the virtual-tryon plugin's one-shot setup.

A reference harness without a vertical is a toy; a vertical skill without a deployable artifact is a slide; a deployable agent without a reference pattern is a prototype no one can repeat. Shipping all three in one repository, under a shared manifest schema and governance pipeline, lets a developer or a coding assistant walk the stack in either direction, with every Agent Platform surface reading from the same source of truth.

The practical result is a lower barrier from "I need an agent that does X" to a running production service: a coding assistant can scaffold a Horizon-shaped agent, install a vertical Plugin Recipe, and reach the deployment transcripts in contrib/ without translating between repositories or reconciling manifest formats. For teams building vertical solutions, Plugin Recipes package domain expertise once and distribute it to every coding assistant on the market with the same install flow and quality gates.

Not an officially supported Google product. Recipes are for demonstration and as starting points, not production use.

#10142. Shipping huggingface_hub every week with AI, open tools, and a human in the loop

huggingface_hub is the Python client at the base of the Hugging Face ecosystem. transformers, datasets, diffusers, sentence-transformers and dozens of other libraries depend on it to talk to the Hub. Every week we don't ship a new release is a week of fixes and features stuck on main.

For a long time we released every 4 to 6 weeks. We now release every week from a single GitHub Actions workflow. We built it using open-source tools and open-weights models and kept a human in the loop at the one place where judgment matters. Nothing in this post requires a vendor contract, a closed model, or infrastructure you can't run yourself. That was a design goal from the start since we wanted a workflow other maintainers could pick up and adapt.

By the end of this post, you'll have everything you need to build your own.

The old process was partly automated, mostly manual.

Writing good notes for a new version was the heavy part, aggregating tens of PRs on different topics. Nothing technically hard but a few hours of focused attention. Add the announcements on top and a minor release was easily a half-day of work spread over several days.

So we decided to streamline the whole thing. Looking at that list, the work splits in two.

Some steps are purely mechanical and can be automated: bumping the version, committing, tagging, pushing, opening downstream test branches, opening the post-release PR. Nobody needs to think about those. They just have to happen in the right order, every time, which is what a CI workflow is good at.

The rest is different. Writing release notes, deciding what to highlight, phrasing an announcement for a human audience: that's brain work. It's the kind of judgment that kept the release manual for years. This is where AI comes in, turning a blank page into a solid first draft in seconds. It's also where we have to be careful because a draft that looks confident and is subtly wrong is worse than no draft at all.

When we decided to fix this, we set one constraint up front: every moving part had to be something any maintainer could run themselves. No closed model behind an API we couldn't swap, no proprietary release platform, no secret sauce.

The second principle: the model drafts, a human decides. Language models are good at turning thirty terse PR titles into readable release notes. They are not good at being trusted blindly. So the workflow is human-supervised: the model does the first pass, a deterministic script checks its work, and a human reviews and edits before anything ships (more on that below).

The full workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/release.yml, triggered by hand from the Actions UI. It takes exactly one input:

From there, the jobs run roughly in this order:

The remaining manual steps are reviewing and publishing the draft release notes, and reviewing and posting an internal Slack message. Those two steps are where we want a human in the loop.

Here's the failure mode everyone worries about with AI-generated release notes: the model quietly drops a PR or invents one that isn't in this release. A changelog that's almost right is worse than no changelog because nobody re-checks it.

We don't trust the generated release notes to be complete on the first try, we verify it deterministically. Before the model runs, a Python script retrieves all PRs that belong to the release and stores them as ground truth.

Then model drafts the notes from them. Once done, we check its output against the initial list of PRs:

If anything is missing or extra, we don't fail and we don't ship a wrong file. We hand the discrepancy back to the agent and ask it to fix exactly those PRs:

This is the pattern that makes the whole thing trustworthy: a non-deterministic model wrapped in deterministic guardrails. The model is great at writing prose and unreliable at being exhaustive. So we let it write and let code enforce the consistency.

Completeness is one half. Accuracy is the other. A model summarizing a PR from its title alone will cheerfully invent a code example that doesn't match the real API.

To prevent that, when we fetch PR metadata we also pull the actual documentation diffs from each PR: the unified diff of any .md file under docs/ that the PR touched.

That diff goes into the model's context so when it writes "here's the new CLI command," it's quoting the example the PR author actually wrote in the docs. That's the same logic as before: give the model real source material and a narrow job.

The prompts themselves live as Skills: small Markdown files (SKILL.md plus reference templates) checked into the repo. The release-notes skill spells out how to pick highlights, how to structure sections, when to add a doc link, etc. It reads like onboarding instructions, which is exactly the right mental model.

After the RC is published, the draft GitHub release sits there with the AI's first pass in it. This is where the human comes in:

The reviewer's time goes into polishing, turning a half-day of writing into a fifteen-minute editing session.

We also keep a paper trail to improve over time. We archive two files side by side to a Hugging Face Bucket: the raw AI draft, uploaded at RC time before anyone touches it, and the human-edited version, uploaded when the final release is cut.

Collecting both every week gives us a growing dataset of "what the model wrote" versus "what we wished it wrote". Dataset that we can then reuse to update the agent's skill.

Revamping the release process was a good opportunity to tighten security, especially against supply-chain attacks.

No PyPI token. Publishing uses Trusted Publishing: PyPI verifies a short-lived OIDC token minted by GitHub for this exact workflow, and issues PEP 740 attestations / Sigstore provenance for every artifact. There's no long-lived secret to leak or rotate.

The agent runtime is pinned and verified. We don't curl | bash the latest OpenCode and hope. We pin a version and check its SHA256 before running it:

Open tooling doesn't mean careless tooling.

Almost nothing. A full release (notes plus the Slack announcement, across 20-40 PRs and a few rounds of prompting) costs about $0.25 on Inference Providers. With open weights billed pay-as-you-go, the only real question each week is "is there something worth shipping?", and there always is.

The cadence went from one release every 4 to 6 weeks to once a week. The secondary effects were the interesting ones:

This is the part we cared about most. The workflow is shaped around huggingface_hub but the structure is generic.

To adapt it: fork the workflow file and scripts, point it at your package, rewrite the skill Markdown for your project's voice, set two repo variables (the model ID and your OpenCode version), set up Trusted Publishing on PyPI, and delete the downstream-testing job if you don't have downstreams. The trust-but-verify loop is the part worth reusing as-is. It's what makes a generated artifact safe to ship.

The parts of a release that used to need a half-day of focused human work (writing notes, drafting announcements, coordinating downstream checks) are the parts a model is good at drafting. Everything else is mechanical and fits in a YAML file. The trick was never just "let the AI do it". It's to let the model draft, let deterministic code verify, and let a human decide. It's built entirely from open tools and open weights so the cost rounds to zero and anyone can run it.

The full workflow file is public. If you maintain a Python library, fork it, adapt it, and let us know how it goes!

Thanks for the post! This will help so many people 🤗

#10140. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

#10138. Dark mode toggles: two states are enough

Exactly the kind of nerdy UI/UX discussion I love:

Lea’s pushing back on light/dark mode implementations that display three state options for visitors:

[…] a good two state control can actually express all three states — users just need to apply the override the first time it becomes relevant.

The first figure succinctly illustrates the point:

In short: No preference? Fall back to the system settings and provide a setting to override that if that’s needed/preferred. Then that preference is stored in localStorage for future sessions.

Something I sorta missed the first time I saw the image is that perhaps we don’t even need to display two states when we know what color scheme is active:

Personally, I’m convinced. Less UI that accomplishes the same as more UI is generally a good thing. Lea’s point goes way beyond that, getting into well-considered reasons that go beyond simplicity.

An interesting consideration is what happens when toggling back to a state. Like, if we start with a Light system preference, toggle it to Dark, then back to Light. Do we get a new override preference or go back to the system setting would be an undefined localStorage value? Maybe it doesn’t matter because theme switching isn’t exactly the primary user intent:

Remember, this control is entirely tangential to the actual user goal for visiting the website. Even if their intent were to pin light instead of reverting to System (light), this is something they would only notice once these diverge, i.e. the OS switches to dark. At that point, fixing it is a single click away. It’s such an easy fix, that there is no point in dwelling on it further.

To be clear, Lea is referring to persistent UI. The guidance is targeting toggles that are always visible to the visitor. That’s really, really common in a site’s header/navigation (my personal site included). If that’s the pattern, then it could distract from the visitor’s primary intent. And the more options we see, the more cognitive dissonance is introduced.

I think there’s an even more compelling argument in the thread:

All I ever wanted was for my OS to be dark, not every website I look at. It was a huge leap by the browser vendors to tie all web content to that system preference.Anyway, I think the light/dark preference should be in the browser, and what you propose seems perfectly in line with that.

Yes, please! Development for the preference, but no need to show an override when the setting is in the browser itself. Then a tri-state toggle might be more acceptable.

Speaking of which, Lea does offer two scenarios where three states make sense:

Update: Lea has published a follow-up that summarizes the whole discussion her first post stirred up. What’s left to say? It’s that this guidance is purely for persistent toggles, such as those in a main navigation. If that’s the case, then her two-state pattern is the way to go. But the best solution? Maybe no toggle at all and let the system default do the work.

We've got lots of ways to help you connect with the greatest front-end community in all the land.

Sign up to get front-end roundups, browser updates, and exclusive content sent to your inbox bi-weekly.

I thought Lea’s approach was very interesting, but I couldn’t get past the fact it feels too magical and a degree of control feels to be lost.

I took a different approach presenting the three options (light/dark/system) with only two buttons and some different behaviour: https://vale.rocks/micros/20260810-0330

I have to respectfully disagree with this approach.

First of all, a three-button segmented control does not take up enough screen real estate to justify removing it. More importantly, this design sacrifices a core UX paradigm for the sake of minimalism: always make it clear to the user what the current state is and what will happen next.

By hiding the “System” state inside a two-state toggle, you create a dynamic deadlock. If my OS is currently in Dark Mode and I want to re-enable the automatic system sync for tomorrow morning, I literally cannot select it because the toggle is already showing “Dark”. A good UI must always allow users to express an intent for the future, rather than just reacting to the present moment. Transparency and control will always beat “clever” hidden logic.

I also prefer the “explicit” 3-state approach.

Bramus eloquently explains why it might be better – https://www.bram.us/2026/08/18/the-case-for-tri-state-dark-mode-toggles/

There’s also a nice article by Bramus on a counterpoint to the two states argument. He argues in favour of the tri-state. https://www.bram.us/2026/08/18/the-case-for-tri-state-dark-mode-toggles/

After reading both, I’m leaning into the tri-state UX.

#10136. Introducing the FFASR Leaderboard: Benchmarking ASR in the Real World

🚀 First open far-field ASR benchmark: community-driven evaluation across 14 simulated rooms, validated against real-world measurements: https://huggingface.co/spaces/treble-technologies/ffasr

📉 The gap is real and it is large: across all submitted models, far-field WER at low SNR is consistently several times higher than near-field WER on the same speech content

🔬 Methodology you can trust: hybrid wave-based simulation, sim-to-real validation, moving-source splits in beta, held-out audio, and standardized evaluation hardware across all submissions

⚡ Accuracy and speed together: the Pareto front plots average WER against RTFx so you can evaluate the tradeoff that is right for your deployment

👀 More is coming: multi-talker scenarios, microphone array support, and echo cancellation are on the roadmap

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment is one of the more persistent frustrations in ASR development. Models that score well on standard evaluations often behave differently once real room acoustics are involved: reverberation, background noise, microphone distance. The complex interactions between these factors affect performance in ways that clean-speech benchmarks do not capture. The FFASR Leaderboard is our attempt to quantify that gap.

Treble Technologies and Hugging Face are launching the Far-Field ASR (FFASR) Leaderboard, the first open, community-driven benchmark designed to evaluate ASR models under realistic far-field acoustic conditions. It is live now, and we are inviting the community to submit models, explore the results, and help shape what comes next.

Voice interfaces have expanded well beyond the headset and the smartphone. AI voice agents, conference room transcription, in-car assistants, humanoid robots, smart glasses, and hands-free tools are all seeing rapid adoption. What they have in common is that they operate in acoustically complex environments: reverberation, background noise, overlapping sounds, and a microphone that may be anywhere from one to several meters from the speaker.

The dominant ASR evaluation paradigm has not caught up with this reality. Clean, close-microphone benchmarks remain the standard, and while they are useful for measuring core recognition quality, they do not predict far-field performance. A model that performs well on LibriSpeech or other near-field sets may degrade substantially once real room acoustics enter the picture. While there have been several research efforts around far-field and noisy speech evaluation — including CHiME, URGENT, and NOIZEUS — the community has not had a standardized, open way to measure that degradation consistently across models in a continuously updated leaderboard format. That is what FFASR is built for.

A major challenge of far-field evaluation is the availability of data. Collecting far-field recordings across a representative range of room types, microphone distances, and noise conditions at scale is prohibitively expensive with physical measurements alone. Simulation makes it possible to cover that space systematically and to extend coverage over time without a corresponding increase in measurement cost.

Another goal of FFASR is to encourage the development of models that are explicitly robust to these conditions. Leaderboards have historically been effective at directing research effort. By making far-field performance visible and comparable, we hope to raise the priority of real-world acoustic robustness across the field.

The FFASR Leaderboard evaluates models across nine conditions. The four that determine the primary ranking score are (as of 22 June 2026):

To give a sense of what these conditions actually sound like, the samples below let you hear the same speech utterance as dry anechoic audio, then convolved with a room impulse response, and finally with noise added at each SNR tier. The difference between the dry recording and the low-SNR far-field condition is a reasonable proxy for the scale of the problem the leaderboard is measuring.

Two additional columns, Lab Measured and Lab Simulated, serve as a sim-to-real validation track. The leaderboard also includes moving-source splits, currently in beta, which evaluate models against audio where the speaker is in motion rather than stationary. This condition reflects use cases such as humanoid robots, in-car speech, and mobile voice assistants where the acoustic geometry between speaker and microphone changes continuously.

The acoustic data is generated with Treble's hybrid simulation engine, which combines a wave-based solver at low to mid frequencies with geometrical-acoustics modeling at higher frequencies. This approach captures physical phenomena that simpler simulation methods often miss: diffraction, scattering, interference, and modal behavior. The result is simulated data that closely matches measured acoustic conditions, which the Lab Measured and Lab Simulated columns confirm directly by running the same evaluation on both.

Fourteen fully furnished rooms are included in the benchmark, ranging from 20 to 470 m³ and covering bathrooms, living rooms with hallways, offices, classrooms, and restaurant spaces. Each acoustic scene contains one target speaker, recorded in an anechoic chamber to avoid reverberation artifacts from the recording environment, and up to three noise sources. Every scene includes both a transient noise source such as coughing and a continuous noise source such as HVAC, at three SNR levels. This coverage is designed to reflect the actual variety of spaces where deployed voice systems operate.

Alongside WER, the leaderboard reports RTFx (audio seconds per inference second) for every submission, evaluated on an NVIDIA L4 GPU under identical conditions. Accuracy and latency together are what matter in real deployments, and the Pareto front view in the Analysis tab makes that tradeoff explicit.

This benchmark is build on simulated acoustic spaces via Treble Technologies proprietaty simulation engine. An example of the output from the enginge can be found in the Treble10 dataset released last year, which established the simulation pipeline and made far-field RIRs available for training and research. FFASR extends that foundation into a standardized evaluation framework with a held-out test set, consistent normalization, and automated scoring.

With the leaderboard live, a consistent pattern is emerging across all submitted models: the gap between near-field and far-field performance is large, and it grows significantly as SNR decreases. Near-field WER values, on clean dry speech, look comparable to what the same models achieve on established benchmarks. Far-field WER at low SNR tells a different story, often several times higher. The benchmark makes this degradation visible and comparable in a way that was previously difficult to do outside proprietary evaluation pipelines.

The Pareto front of average WER against RTFx is also revealing. There is a genuine spectrum of approaches represented in the current submissions: models that prioritize speed at the cost of some accuracy, models that push accuracy at the cost of throughput, and a smaller number that achieve a competitive position on both axes. Visualizing these tradeoffs against far-field accuracy rather than clean-speech accuracy produces a materially different picture of where the real differences between systems lie. The Analysis tab is worth exploring beyond the main ranking table.

One observation worth highlighting for developers: the leaderboard reports both near-field (dry) and far-field WER side by side. This separation is intentional and useful. It makes it possible to distinguish between a model that is genuinely accurate and one that is accurate but brittle to acoustic conditions, which matters for deciding whether to invest in far-field fine-tuning, speech enhancement preprocessing, or a different architecture altogether.

Open the Submit tab on the FFASR Leaderboard, paste a Hugging Face model ID, and evaluation runs server-side against the held-out dataset. The pipeline supports Whisper variants, IBM Granite Speech, Cohere Transcribe, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT CTC heads, SpeechBrain ASR, and most other ASR architectures on the Hub without any custom configuration.

For teams using more complex inference stacks, including systems that combine speech enhancement with ASR, a custom evaluator option allows you to define your own evaluate() function. Custom evaluators run on Hub Jobs after moderator review, and the submission notes field is a good place to document any preprocessing steps so results are interpretable by others.

The held-out evaluation set uses 2,000 anechoic speech samples across 14 rooms at three SNR tiers, approximately 8 hours of audio per condition, with Whisper-style text normalization applied consistently. The audio is not exposed to submitters, to avoid test-set contamination.

The conditions we are actively exploring for future tracks include multi-talker scenarios, where more than one speaker is active simultaneously, microphone array evaluation, covering beamforming and spatial filtering approaches, and echo cancellation, relevant for any device that plays audio while also listening.

What we build next will depend on where the community tells us the gaps are largest. If you work on a deployment environment or a use case that is not well represented in the current benchmark, we want to hear from you. The FFASR Leaderboard is designed to grow, and the direction it grows should reflect real needs.

Submit your model, explore the Analysis tab, post your ideas and suggestions on the FFASR forum, and help us build a benchmark that is actually useful for the problems the field is working on.

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

Btw one related idea I've had sitting on the back of my mind: there's a class of synthetic audio scenarios that don't really occur naturally but are both tricky and relevant to real deployments.

Most ASR models lately seem geared toward clean meeting transcription. But if you run a Granola style setup that pulls every audio stream on your machine and mixes them together, things get messy fast. The system audio from the meeting, your physical hardware mic, and sometimes your own voice echoing back through the meeting can all be mixed/delayed/noisy in the same track the model sees. (I use VibeVoice for this myself since I figured it would be more robust; it's held up okay, but I haven't done a real comparison)

Mixed multi-stream audio like that feels like a natural fit for the kind of robustness/"real world scenario" this benchmark is measuring, even though it's a synthetic condition rather than a recorded room

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

#10133. WordPress.com Student Plan

So happy to see WordPress.com offering a pricing tier aimed at students that gives them free hosting for a year:

WordPress.com offers the Student plan free, so cost is never a barrier to learning web skills. The goal is for students of any subject to create and share their thoughts and work online, and to own their online presence from the start.

I also think it’s way overdue. As someone who teaches beginning web development, I find that building a WordPress site makes for a great final project to demonstrate the myriad skills covered over the course of a semester — HTML, CSS, design, hosting, etc. Hosting those projects has always been a roadblock though.

I’ve tried several othered things over the years: Shared hosting plans (which sets me back financially), WPSandox.io (gone bye-bye though there are alternatives), WordPress Playground (saving and sharing work is complicated), sponsored hosting (it’s a hard sell on a semester-by-semester basis), and on and on.

A student plan with a year-long leash straight from the source is the perfect solution. You might think that WordPress.com is too point-and-click compared to a self-hosted WordPress.org site, but dot-com offers all the same developer affordances for directly touching code these days.

It’s worth noting that the deal is only good for .blog and .art domains. Not a deal-breaker whatsoever when it comes to educational purposes. You can always point it elsewhere down the road if you want to spend a few bucks.

I do not agree. I think it an accident waiting to happen. Read my blog post here:

https://www.usecue.com/blog/wordpress-com-student-plan/

I read your post (nicely written!) but didn’t exactly see an explanation for why a student plan is a disaster waiting to happen.

Your core concerns appear to be: (1) limited development capability, and (2) security.

(1) The student plan still allows learners to touch code as you can any self-hosted WordPress site, complete with developer tools and access. I’ve said it in this post, but I’ve taught the core tenants of web fundamentals for years. It’s not about learning WordPress, but using WordPress as a platform for demonstrating those fundamentals. And if learners are capable of touching the code — as they can — then it’s capable of demonstrating retained learning objectives.

(2) WordPress is only singled out by those concerned about security because it’s the largest and most adopted CMS, by far. Every platform (minus static generators, I suppose) carry the same risks. WordPress aggressively releases security updates and I think it’s great that WordPress.com handles the updating overhead for users.

And I’m less concerned about plugin vulnerabilities as a whole, because the final project for my course does not rely on them. The project is designed to assess core web fundamentals rather than extending a CMS.

But that’s my course, specifically. It’s totally valid if you are teaching for different learning outcomes that would validate your concerns.

#10132. AI-Powered Pentesting for DevSecOps: 7 Checks Developers Should Make First

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Security testing used to happen once or twice a year, usually after a release had already shipped. That rhythm does not fit teams that deploy daily. AI-assisted tools now promise testing that runs continuously, chains steps together on its own, and writes up what it found.

For developers, the interesting question is not whether these tools are impressive. It is what has to be true in your pipeline before you let an automated attacker loose on your own systems. This article covers seven checks to make first, each with a pass condition, and one short code example you can run. Some checks, such as written authorization and cost tracking, usually belong to a security lead or manager. For those, the developer's job is to confirm they exist, not to own them.

Testing systems you do not have permission to test is not a gray area. Make sure someone with authority has approved the targets and the time window, and keep that approval with your records. Run the first tests against staging with test data. Production comes later, once you know how the tool behaves and what load it creates.

Pass: The approval is on file, and the SOC knows the window and source IPs.

An automated tester should never decide for itself what it is allowed to touch. Define scope in a file that your pipeline can check: which hosts are in bounds, when testing may run, and whether anything destructive is allowed.

SitePoint's article on security patterns for autonomous agents uses an open-source AI penetration-testing agent as its case study. It covers sandboxed execution, tool permissions scoped to each role, approval gates for high-risk actions, and audit logging. Scope enforcement belongs in that same family of controls. Here is a minimal check that refuses any target outside the allowlist or time window:

Call this before every scan job, and log the result. A tool that is out of bounds should fail loudly instead of quietly continuing.

Pass: An out-of-scope target fails the job, and egress outside the allowlist is blocked.

Findings are only useful if they reach the people who can fix them. Most teams already have a place where security results show up in pull requests or a security tab. SitePoint's walkthrough on automating DevSecOps static analysis with GitHub Actions shows how results written in the SARIF format appear as inline annotations and can block a merge when severity crosses a threshold. If your pentest tool can export SARIF or a similar format, send its findings to the same place.

Pass: The tool exports SARIF or similar, and results show up in PRs or the security tab.

An AI tool can produce a long list of findings. To judge whether they are complete and sensible, you need a reference for what good web security testing covers. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is a free, widely used checklist of test categories for web applications. It covers web applications only, so APIs and network services exposed to the internet need their own coverage. Map the tool's findings against it, and note which categories it never touched.

Pass: You know which OWASP WSTG categories you expect the tool to cover.

Vendors describe AI pentesting in similar terms: agents plan attack steps, try them, and verify what works. For a view of how a security vendor explains the approach, CyCognito's overview of AI penetration testing walks through a workflow from scoping to autonomous testing, validation and reporting, and notes that human review stays part of the process. All vendor claims need testing in a demo against your own systems before you rely on them.

Ask the same questions of any tool you evaluate: What does it test beyond known checks? How does it confirm a finding is real? What does it send to external services?

Pass: The vendor has clear answers, including where the target list comes from.

Automated findings need review. A person should confirm that a reported path is exploitable, judge its business impact, and decide the fix order. Make sure this is set up before the first run. Without it, a team can end up with a long backlog of unverified findings and little trust in the tool.

Pass: There is a named reviewer and time set aside each cycle.

Running agents continuously can add up, especially when they call large models. Make sure you can track what each run costs and how many real issues it finds, so you can compare it with other approaches. You also need to be able to rerun the specific test that found a problem after a fix ships and keep the result. A finding is only closed when the retest passes.

Pass: Both are possible before you commit to running the tool continuously.

Does AI pentesting replace manual penetration testing?

Not entirely. Automated testing can run more often and cover more ground, but people are still needed for scoping, complex attack paths and judging impact.

In staging, with test data, inside a written scope and time window.

What should I do with findings from the tool?

Send them to the same place as your other security results, have the named reviewer check them, and retest after fixes.

AI-assisted pentesting can give development teams faster and more frequent security feedback, but only when it runs inside clear limits. Before the first run, check that targets and the window are approved, scope is enforced by your pipeline, findings will land where developers work, you have a baseline to judge the output, you know what the tool tests and sends out, someone owns the review, and you can measure cost and retest. The scope check above is small, but it makes sure the tool stays inside the lines you set.

#10131. Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API

Shipping on-device AI means meeting tight latency and memory budgets on every device you target. The most common path for deploying models in production is converting a trained model, for example converting a PyTorch model with LiteRT Torch, and running it with the LiteRT runtime. This offers the quickest and most reliable route to production, and it's the path we recommend for most projects. Sometimes, though, developers want full control over how a network is represented and optimized to support new architectures or to try a new lowering logic without waiting for upstream framework updates.

For ultimate control, developers write computations manually in native C++ or shader languages. Apple's MLX made this code-first approach popular on Apple silicon, and llama.cpp showed how far tailored C++ implementations can take LLM inference. However, the level of control comes at a significant cost: implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.

To solve the above challenges, we are excited to announce the release of the novel LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight authoring layer in the LiteRT stack, designed to improve handcrafting models. It combines the flexibility of native authoring with cross-platform portability. You build the computation graph op by op in C++, choosing exactly which ops run and how they connect. The same graph can run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU (powered by open-source ML Drift) and NPU, or without model file or runtime directly on CPU through XNNPACK, so you don't rewrite it for each new hardware target. Model inference and pre/post-processing can be assembled with the same API and chained through shared accelerator buffers, so that data never round-trips through the CPU. Start with the conversion path, which remains the best default for most models. Reach for the Tensor API when you need low-level control over the graph or want the whole pipeline to run end to end on the accelerator.

The LiteRT Tensor API also serves as an ideal programmatic foundation for AI coding agents, providing structured primitives to generate, rewire, and tune model graphs automatically. In the rest of this post, we’ll dive into the design and walk through practical code examples showing how to author models from scratch.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

To show the Tensor API in practice, we built an interactive Segment Anything App, running entirely on-device in the browser on WebGPU. The app enables real-time multi-object segmentation and tracking via Meta's Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2), triggered either by simple clicks or natural language prompts powered by Gemma 4 E2B.

The SAM 2 model is fully authored in C++ via the LiteRT Tensor API. A coding agent wrote and evolved it from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU. See that the complete implementation and the web app are open source in the LiteRT Samples GitHub repo.

The LiteRT Tensor API provides four key features for authoring and optimizing on-device models:

We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder). The SAM 2.1 sample includes the benchmark commands so you can reproduce the results.

With the Tensor API, each layer is a C++ function over Tensor values, built from high-level operators and weights loaded directly from the checkpoint. For example, here is a multi-head self-attention layer:

In the SAM 2 sample, BuildEncoder and BuildDecoder compose layers like this into the encoder and decoder graphs, and ModelFactory exports both as two signatures of one sam2_image.tflite file.

A .tflite file is one of two ways to run your graph. The backend is a template argument on Tensor: TfLiteMixinTag exports a .tflite that LiteRT runs on CPU, ML Drift (GPU), or NPU, and XnnpackMixinTag runs the same code directly on CPU through XNNPACK, with no model file. Tag tensors with both to keep both options:

SAM 2 takes the .tflite path to reach WebGPU in the browser, and the rest of this post follows it. The Gemma 4 example takes the direct path for prefill and decode on CPU, the lightest way to run Tensor API code. The Tensor API README walks through both.

A natural workflow uses both: iterate on the direct XNNPACK path, loading weights straight from the .safetensors checkpoint with no model file to rebuild, then export a .tflite when you're ready to ship with LiteRT on mobile or on the web through LiteRT.js.

A real app needs more than the neural network itself. In the demo, turning a camera frame and a click into a mask takes four steps: pre-processing converts the frame into the 512x512 image the model expects; the image encoder turns that image into features; the mask decoder combines those features with the click to predict a mask; and post-processing scales the mask back to the frame's size. Running this whole pipeline fast takes two things: keeping data on the accelerator (such as the GPU) between steps, and controlling how each step runs on each accelerator.

In a typical app, only the model runs on the GPU; the CPU resizes each camera frame, passes the encoder's output to the decoder, and post-processes the mask. Each trip copies data and stalls the GPU.

In litert-samples/sam2, all four steps are Tensor API graphs on the GPU. Pre-processing, for example, is a small graph built with CreateLambdaRunner. The graphs are connected once at startup to share buffers, then run for each frame and click:

No data returns to the CPU between steps: all 522 encoder and 269 decoder operations run on the GPU, and pre- and post-processing add only about 0.34 ms per frame.

Because the graph is plain C++, you or your coding agent can rewrite it for each backend. Our agent, Antigravity, moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph. Comparisons like score > 0 would still fall back to the CPU on WebGPU, because they output true/false values, so the agent rewrote them as arithmetic in StepPos:

Each object now takes a single GPU call per frame. The agent made a series of changes like this, such as folding the attention scale into the weights, and checked each against Hugging Face's SAM 2 before keeping it. That's how we more than tripled the model's frame rate.

We're working on direct ML Drift (GPU) backends, NPU-friendly operations, and automatic full-graph quantization. We're also adding Python authoring with .tflite export, plus wider dynamic-shape support for varying image sizes, batch sizes, and sequence lengths.

Explore our resources and start your journey with LiteRT:

The LiteRT Tensor API and its reference implementations are the result of a collaborative effort across the Google AI Edge and LiteRT teams. Special thanks to Byungchul Kim, Changming Sun, Chenchen Tang, Dillon Sharlet, Jingjiang Li, Lu Wang, Lutz Justen, Matthias Grundmann, Misha Gutman, Ronald Wotzlaw, and Sachin Kotwani.

#10130. Accelerating Transformers Fine-Tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel

HuggingFace Transformers has become the foundation of the open-source AI ecosystem, and the recent Transformers v5 release strengthened it with first-class support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, now the dominant architecture for frontier models. v5 ships the MoE foundations: expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and distributed execution that make MoE extensible and easy to build on.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is an open library part of the NVIDIA NeMo framework for building custom generative AI models at scale. NeMo AutoModel builds cleanly on top of v5, adding Expert Parallelism, DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels, and it leans on v5's dynamic weight loading to bring those optimizations to a broad and growing set of model families. The payoff is 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput and 29-32% less GPU memory on fine-tuning MoE models than native Transformers v5, using the same from_pretrained() API: a single import line, with no other code changes.

This blog details how this combination works and how users can fine-tune MoE models faster without changing their APIs.

The rise of MoE models has introduced new challenges to efficient training: Routing tokens across hundreds of experts, fusing expert matmuls into a single kernel, sharding weights across GPUs, and overlapping communication with computation all require infrastructure beyond what a general-purpose library provides out of the box.

Transformers v5 (“v5”) introduced first-class MoE support such as expert backends, dynamic weight loading, and tensor parallel plans for distributed execution. In addition, v5 made distributed training first-class by integrating PyTorch's DeviceMesh directly into from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel builds on top of v5 by subclassing AutoModelForCausalLM, and adding Expert Parallelism (EP), DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch, and TransformerEngine kernels. DeepEP is the piece v5 doesn't have yet: it overlaps communication with expert compute. And because NeMo AutoModel rides v5's reversible weight conversion to load each model, it can focus its engineering on these reusable core ops instead of per-model checkpoint plumbing, while save_pretrained() still emits standard HF checkpoints that tools like vLLM and SGLang can load.

The next section walks through how the two work together and the performance gains we measured, from full fine-tuning NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B across 16 nodes down to single-node models such as Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B.

One of NeMo AutoModel's goals is API compatibility with HuggingFace Transformers to enable open-source community. NeMoAutoModelForCausalLM subclasses AutoModelForCausalLM, so any code that works with HF models works with AutoModel too.

Here's what loading a model looks like in both. Only the import changes:

That single import does a lot of work. For popular MoE architectures like Qwen3, NVIDIA Nemotron, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek V3, NeMo AutoModel ships hand-tuned implementations with TransformerEngine attention, fused linear layers, and custom expert kernels. For everything else, it falls back to vanilla HF while still applying optimizations like Liger kernel patching, among others. And whichever path it takes, the resulting model is ready to scale: pass a device_mesh and you have multi-GPU training without further rewrites.

Where NeMo AutoModel really shines is scaling MoE models to multi-GPU training. To train Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with Expert Parallelism across 8 GPUs, one adds the distributed mesh configuration:

This gives speed, scalability and memory-optimizations with FSDP2, Expert Parallelism, TransformerEngine kernels and DeepEP dispatch, all from a from_pretrained() call.

We evaluated NeMo AutoModel in two regimes: full fine-tuning a frontier-scale 550B model across 16 nodes, and training two 30B MoE models on a single node. The 550B result shows why Expert Parallelism is essential at scale; the 30B results quantify the per-GPU speedup over Transformers v5.

Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B is a 550B-parameter hybrid model shipping with Mamba2, LatentMoE, and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). We benchmark a full fine-tune: every parameter is updated and the Adam optimizer state is materialized, which at this scale spans 16 H100 nodes (128 GPUs).

Why there is no Transformers v5 column. Transformers v5 runs out of memory at this scale, so there is no v5 number to report here. AutoModel's Expert Parallelism shards the experts across GPUs to bring the footprint within budget, which is what lets the full fine-tune run. The 30B comparisons below show the same advantage where v5 fits.

We benchmarked three approaches on a single node with 8x H100 80GB GPUs: HF Transformers v4 (hub code), HF Transformers v5 (with best available optimizations), and NeMo AutoModel (EP=8 + custom kernels).

A note on the routing gate. The NeMo AutoModel numbers below use a balanced routing gate, which forces tokens to be distributed uniformly across experts. This emulates the ideal operating point an MoE is trained toward: a well-trained model's load-balancing loss drives expert utilization to near-uniform, so balanced routing reflects the steady-state a real workload converges to (and removes the straggler noise that random dummy tokens otherwise inject into expert parallelism). v4/v5 run their native router on the same dummy tokens. The balanced gate therefore measures NeMo AutoModel at its target MoE operating point, and the v4/v5 columns reflect their out-of-the-box behavior.

Why v4 deadlocks: Transformers v4 stores Qwen3 MoE experts as a ModuleList of 128 individual MLP modules, each separately FSDP-wrapped. The forward pass uses a data-dependent loop that only iterates experts that received tokens. With different data per rank, different ranks skip different experts, causing mismatched FSDP AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives and an indefinite hang. Transformers v5 fixes this by storing experts as fused 3D parameter tensors (no per-expert modules, no per-expert FSDP collectives).

v4 config: trust_remote_code=True (NVIDIA's hub modeling code). The hub code's expert loop is FSDP-safe (iterates all experts regardless of token assignment), so it doesn't deadlock like Qwen3 v4.

The 3.4-3.7x speedup from NeMo AutoModel over Transformers v5 comes from three sources:

Expert Parallelism reduces memory pressure. EP=8 distributes expert weights across GPUs, cutting the per-GPU MoE footprint by 8x. For Qwen3, this drops peak memory from 68.2 GiB to 48.1 GiB (-29%). For Nemotron Nano, it drops from 62.1 GiB to 42.5 GiB (-32%), freeing headroom for larger batch sizes or longer sequences.

DeepEP fuses communication with computation. Instead of separate AllGather/ReduceScatter collectives for expert routing, DeepEP fuses token dispatch and combines into optimized GPU kernels, overlapping communication with expert computation.

TransformerEngine kernels accelerate core operations. TE's fused attention, linear layers, and RMSNorm implementations provide consistent speedups over their PyTorch/Flash Attention equivalents across all layer types, not just MoE layers.

One of the most impactful features in Transformers v5 is the experts_implementation parameter, which includes three expert backends:

The grouped_mm backend is the key training optimization: instead of looping over experts one by one, it sorts tokens by their assigned expert and executes a single fused grouped matrix multiplication.

NeMo AutoModel takes this further. For models with custom implementations, it uses DeepEP fused all-to-all dispatch combined with grouped GEMM kernels and TransformerEngine linear layers. The progression looks like:

In NeMo AutoModel, the expert backend is configured through BackendConfig:

Transformers v5 also ships an Expert Parallelism path. It shards expert weights across GPUs. The GroupedGemmParallel style loads only each device's local experts, and RouterParallel routes tokens and combines results with an all_reduce. It's neatly built on v5's existing tensor-parallel machinery. Enabling it makes the model's tp_plan return its expert plan, so expert parallelism shares the device budget with data parallelism (ep × dp = world_size). For the single-node 30B benchmarks here, we found plain data-parallel v5 (dp=8, ep=1) to be the fastest v5 configuration, so that's the v5 setup we report.

NeMo AutoModel takes a complementary approach tuned for multi-GPU MoE training. It makes EP its own parallelism dimension, a dedicated moe_mesh alongside (rather than carved from) the data-parallel mesh, using PyTorch's DTensor with Shard(0). Because the expert mesh is orthogonal to data parallelism, the two compose on the same devices. On 8 GPUs NeMo AutoModel runs ep=8 and dp=8 together, so every GPU trains on its own data shard while holding only 1/8 of the experts. Expert weights are physically sharded across GPUs along the expert dimension.

With ep_size=8 on 8 GPUs, each GPU holds only 1/8 of the expert parameters. For a model like Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B with ~55 GiB of expert weights, EP reduces the per-GPU expert footprint from ~55 GiB to ~6.8 GiB, making training possible where FSDP-only approaches run out of memory.

On top of EP, NeMo AutoModel integrates DeepEP that fuses the token routing into optimized GPU kernels, and delivers significant speedups when combined with grouped GEMM for grouped expert computation. In our large-scale MoE benchmarks, DeepEP + grouped GEMM reduced cost per iteration by 47% on the full DeepSeek V3 671B model compared to all-gather + looped expert baselines.

Transformers v5 also introduced a dynamic weight loading system through WeightConverter and WeightRenaming. This enables MoE checkpoint to be stored in fused 3D tensors for more efficient execution. The WeightConverter applies composable operations to transform checkpoint tensors on-the-fly during from_pretrained().

NeMo AutoModel is a direct consumer of this v5 API. Over 20 model types use this mechanism through MODELS_REQUIRING_TENSOR_MERGING, including Mixtral, Qwen2 MoE, Qwen3 MoE, DeepSeek V2/V3, OLMoE, and more. The conversions are fully reversible: save_pretrained() produces standard HF-format checkpoints that any downstream tool can load.

To try NeMo AutoModel, please visit our official documentation page to get started.

NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel is the natural next step for HuggingFace users scaling up model training. By building directly on Transformers v5, AutoModel provides a zero-friction upgrade path: change one import line and get a model instance that is more than three times as fast.

On Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, this delivers 3.4-3.7x higher training throughput with 29-32% less GPU memory compared to the best Transformers v5 configuration. And because true Expert Parallelism shards experts across GPUs, the same path scales up to full fine-tuning a 550B model like Nemotron 3 Ultra across 16 nodes, the regime where Expert Parallelism becomes essential to fit the model in memory. Because NeMo AutoModel checkpoints are standard HF-format safetensors, you can deploy them on inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang.

The code, configs, and benchmark scripts are all available in the NeMo AutoModel repository.

Core contributors to this work, listed alphabetically by last name: Adil Asif, Hemil Desai, Alexandros Koumparoulis, and Huiying Li.

#10128. CSS Navigation Matching, Early Days

Really like the intent here. Apply a style when someone navigates from one specific page to another. The idea being it’d make the sources for cross-document view transitions declarative in CSS rather than managing that stuff in JavaScript.

Bramus has a hypothetical example as this feature is fleshed out:

That’s for when we know the exact pages we’re navigating from and to. There’s URL pattern matching as well for the times we don’t:

There are additional ways to define the @location besides the pathname and url-pattern descriptors. Like maybe you’re trying to match a hash-ed URL instead, or a specific port or hostname. Apparently there’s protocol and search too, but honestly, I’d have to see examples and use cases to understand when to use one descriptor over another.

OK, so then we have a way to query the @navigation between locations using the custom idents registered in the @location. If the navigation matches the two points of navigation, then bingo.

Pretty clean from and to conditions there where they’re connected by an and keyword.

Another way to write it that’s a tad cleaner:

Or, hey, we can fire this off when there is not a match:

There’s also an at keyword to connect locations. The spec draft is vague on this at the moment, but Bramus demonstrates it like this:

I’ve gotta wrap my head around that. The way I read it, it says, “when you’re navigating between --home and --detail and you’re starting ‘at’ --home, select this element and give it this view transition name.” In other words, it happens at the very, very beginning (or end, I suppose) of the navigation between pages rather than when it’s in progress. I think. Please correct me.

And what about that :nav-source pseudo (which may be renamed to :navigation-source)? Again, gotta wrap my head around it all. But if I am understanding right, that’s to match the specific element that triggers the transition. It’s the source of the navigation, be it a link, image, div, or whatever element. I didn’t see anything in the spec draft about a corresponding pseudo that matches the element on the other side of the transition — say, :target? — but perhaps there’s no clear use case for it.

Speaking of pseudos, the spec defines another one called :link-to() that applies styles to a linked element that targets a certain location. Straight from the spec:

…which I imagine matches an element in HTML like:

…which I think is a lot like styling links based on their targeted destination? Maybe it’s more a DX convenience when there’s already a declared location?

One thing I’m already not liking is that I doubt these features would work for a site like CSS-Tricks that has such a flat URL structure. Most of our URLs are a single level deep. So, if I want to match between a specific page (/about) and any article (/article-url) there’s no way to distinguish that route. But maybe that says something about the way URLs are designed around here and they should have more structure. That’s not a trivial change though.

My friend Lee Meyer suggests that perhaps it would be possible to append a a parameter like ?blog on URL to gain URL pattern matching superpowers.

Oh, and while I’m thinking of it, I could see a possible use case where you’d want to apply certain styles when navigating from one specific page to another. Like, maybe you’re navigating between the homepage and an About page and want to style elements on the destination page based on where you’re coming from. Playing off the earlier example from Bramus:

I dunno. Seems like there could be security issues with that?

And Preethi chimed in on the CSS-Tricks Slack channel with what I think is insightful feedback:

It would’ve been great if we had an at-rule for all data infrastructures, similar to @property for all property-value pairs, with configurations valid as per type. We could’ve used it instead of @color-profile, @position-try, and now @location.

So true when there’s so many new rules to learn these days. Anything that lowers the learning curve is certainly worth considering.

You’ll want to peruse the spec draft for yourself to get deeper into the nitty-gritty of things like navigating based on navigation “type” (e.g., back, forward, reload) and navigation “phases” (e.g., loading, ready, committed).

It’s a lot to take in. But so are view transitions as a whole.
